terms.gloss: take someone up in one’s carriage, give someone a lift
terms.grammar: aliquem raedā tollere: tollō, tollere, sustulī, sublātum, with the ablative of the vehicle
evidence: Hor. S. 2.6.42–43: quem tollere raedā vellet iter faciēns
terms.comment: Horace’s phrase for what Maecenas’s friendship first came to: someone he would take along in his carriage on a journey. With autoraedā it says the same of a car.

terms.gloss: take someone up into one’s car, give someone a lift
evidence: Cic. Off. 3.94: optāvit, ut in currum patris tollerētur; sublātus est
Cic. N. D. 3.76: in currum quom Phaethontem fīlium sustulit
terms.comment: Cicero’s words for the Sun taking Phaethon up into his chariot.

evidence: Liv. 5.40: plaustrō conjugem ad līberōs vehēns
terms.comment: The plain verb for carrying someone in a vehicle, with the ablative of the vehicle.

phrases.latin: Vīn' tē raedā tollam? Domum tuam praetervehor.
phrases.english: Shall I give you a lift? I’m driving past your house.

phrases.latin: quem tollere raedā vellet iter faciēns
phrases.english: someone he would be willing to take up in his carriage when travelling

phrases.latin: dēscendere uxōrem ac puerōs jussit, virginēs sacraque in plaustrum imposuit et Caere quō iter sacerdōtibus erat pervexit
phrases.english: he told his wife and children to get down, put the Vestal Virgins and the sacred objects into his cart, and carried them all the way to Caere, where the priestesses were going

sources: Lewis & Short: tollo · Lewis & Short: currus · Lewis & Short: veho
John C. Traupman, Conversational Latin for Oral Proficiency, p. 215.
